newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican bellwether Cetes rate soars on weak peso.
newsitem.headline: Mexican bellwether Cetes rate soars on weak peso.

text.p: Interest rates on Mexico's bellwether one-month Cetes (T-bill) rose sharply at the primary auction on Tuesday in a reaction to the weakening peso, analysts said.
The bellwether one-month paper jumped 316 basis points to 25.90 percent at Banco de Mexico's auction.

It was the first rise in rates after five consecutive weeks of declines that brought real interest rates in Mexico to their lowest levels since before the December 1994 peso crash. Rates rose to their highest levels in two months.
"Obviously the results were due to the pressure from the exchange rate," one Mexico City analyst said.
"The rise in rates was expected, although the pressure on rates was pretty strong -- they could have gone up even more," he said.
A Reuters survey of 11 money market traders before the auction showed they expected the bellwether 28-day Cetes rates to rise by an average of 371 basis points.

The prospect of higher rates helped Mexico's peso to rebound slightly on Tuesday after having fallen from about 7.60 to 7.75 per dollar in recent sessions. On Tuesday it closed at 7.719/7.729 per dollar in 48-hour trade.

Higher rates should keep the peso from weakening further, even though the currency has recently become the focus of debate in Mexico over whether it has gained too much this year following last year's tumble. The peso was also hurt early this week by news the government was backtracking from plans to fully privatise Mexico's secondary petrochemicals industry.
Analysts also said some investors were demanding higher return for Mexican paper ahead of the government's economic program for 1997 -- which has yet to be announced.

The 91-day paper rose 364 basis points to 28.75 percent, while the six-month paper rose 221 basis points to 29.05 percent. The one-year paper yielded 28.65 percent this week after yielding 26.83 percent last week. The rise in the primary rates was prefigured by rising secondary money market rates.

In the secondary market on Tuesday, overnight rates reached a high of 26 percent on expectations that primary rates were about to soar in reaction to liquidity pressures in the secondary market and to shore up the weak peso.
Earlier this week, Banco de Mexico said that it would drain the money market of 20 million pesos a day rather than continue with its neutral stance since August 16.
